# *Signal*.

:::{.callout-important}
## In Brief
Signal is the discipline of refusing to move forward until one constraint has been identified precisely, confirmed against actual numbers, and quantified in dollars or hours. By the time you finish this stage, you have a one-page Constraint Statement that names the problem, where it lives, how long it has existed, and what it has cost.
:::

Jesse was in our own L10, reviewing the scorecard for our project management function. The numbers weren't red, they were blank. Tasks were being created but not updated. Client deliverables were slipping by days without anyone flagging it. Billing was late because nobody could confirm what had been delivered and what hadn't. We were paying a project coordinator $24,000 a year as a subcontractor, and the work was still falling behind.

We asked the room a question we ask clients all the time: what is this costing us? Not the subcontractor's invoice, but the actual cost. The late billing. The missed deliverables. The hours our VP of Operations was spending chasing task updates instead of running operations.

Nobody had the number. We'd been living with the problem long enough that it felt like weather, just the way project coordination worked at our size. The coordinator was failing, but the role was also inadequate. The work required someone in the system constantly, updating tasks and flagging overdue items. No part-time subcontractor was going to sustain that, and hiring a full-time person meant $50,000 or more for work that was largely mechanical.

The real question was whether this was a capacity problem, a capability problem, or whether we could redesign the work itself. That question is what launched us down the path that became Source and Design.

That conversation was the first time we named the constraint instead of the symptom. The symptom was "tasks are falling behind." The constraint was structural: the project coordination function required constant, systematic attention that no human in the role, at the price point we could justify, was going to sustain. Without Signal, teams replace the person, add a person, or build a workaround, and the constraint stays where it was.

Julie has watched the same discipline land outside any AI context. In a post-acquisition integration at a global food safety company, the presenting problem was a talent gap: leadership teams in the acquired division were underperforming against expectations, and the business instinct was to replace several key leaders. Before any replacement decisions were made, Julie ran the equivalent of Signal — what was the actual constraint, where did it live, what was it costing? Tracing the underperformance to its root revealed it was concentrated in roles where two reporting lines crossed, matrix structures inherited from the Fortune 500 parent with no clear decision authority assigned.

The leaders were operating inside an accountability structure that made it impossible to perform. The constraint was how authority was assigned. Signal prevented a series of expensive, wrong decisions and produced a redesign that resolved the performance gap without replacing a single person.

This chapter fills in the Constraint section of your Sprint Planning Canvas, plus the first row of the Sequence first-pass.

## The deliverable is *one sentence*.

Signal produces one artifact: a one-page Constraint Statement. Its single anchoring sentence names the problem, where it lives in the org, how long it has existed, and what it has cost in dollars, time, or margin. The rest of the page surrounds that sentence with the evidence that validates it.

Here's the template. You'll fill it in by the end of this chapter.

{{< excalidraw ch04-constraint-statement-template "Constraint Statement template: one sentence, location, duration, quantified cost, and validating evidence." >}}

The anchoring sentence follows this structure: "[Function] cannot [desired outcome] because [root cause], which costs us approximately [X dollars] per [Y time period]."

That form names the function that's failing, the outcome that's blocked, and the structural cause rather than the symptom. "Elena can't quote within 24 hours because she's the sole holder of customer pricing context, which costs us approximately $558K per year." That's a constraint you can act on.

The discipline of insisting on one is the entire point. You may arrive at this conversation with five candidates. The job of Signal is to refuse the list. You pick one constraint: the one that, if removed, would change the math most meaningfully. You commit to it for the length of the Sprint.

That commitment is structural. A Sprint that tries to solve three problems solves none of them. A Sprint that solves one produces a measurable result against a number you wrote down at the start, and that result becomes the proof point that earns the next Sprint. The narrowness is what makes the work pay.

The quantified cost is non-negotiable. "It's a big problem" is not a constraint. "The quoting bottleneck is costing us $558K per year in lost revenue, misallocated time, and floor underutilization" is. The number does two things. It tells you whether the constraint is worth a Sprint's attention, and it gives you a target the Deliver phase can measure against. Without it, you cannot prove the Sprint paid for itself.

:::{.callout-tip}
## Pro Tip
If you can't put a number on the cost, you haven't found the constraint yet. Keep working. "Significant" is not a number. Neither is "a lot." Hours per week, dollars per quarter, margin lost, deals not closed — pick a unit and estimate it.
:::

## The gate is real. You don't get past it by *declaring* it complete.

Signal is a gate. You don't move to Source until the constraint is locked — one validated Constraint Statement with a number on it.

The most common failure mode is political, not technical. Leadership teams can't agree on which constraint is the constraint, so they punt — they pick three, or they write something so abstract it can't be acted on. If your team can't pick one, you've learned something important before a single line of the Sprint has been built: the leadership team is unclear about priorities. That's upstream of anything in this book.

Signal is locked when the team has a Constraint Statement in writing and everyone in the room agrees that it names the right problem.

## *Symptom* is not the same as *constraint*.

Symptoms are visible. Constraints are structural.

A quoting process that takes too long is a symptom. A messy onboarding is a symptom. Neither one is a constraint a Sprint can solve.

Signal traces the symptom to the underlying constraint. Quoting takes too long because three different systems hold pieces of the customer record, and the ops manager is the only person who knows how to reconcile them. Onboarding is messy because the handoff between sales and delivery is undefined, and every new customer triggers a custom escalation chain.

The same distinction matters in human-capital contexts. "Our managers aren't developing their people" is a symptom we've watched leadership teams treat as a personnel problem for years. The constraint underneath it might be that managers have no time for development conversations because their operational workload has grown to absorb every hour. Or the constraint might be that the performance management system creates no accountability for development outcomes, so development conversations never happen because nothing bad happens when they don't. Without the structural cause and a cost, you're treating weather.

{{< excalidraw ch04-symptom-to-constraint "Symptom to constraint: three complaints traced from the visible symptom to the structural cause and what it costs." >}}

Four patterns reliably surface the structural constraint underneath the symptom:

**Conversations that keep coming up but never get resolved.** If your team has been discussing the same issue for two quarters and nobody has fixed it, the issue is a symptom. The constraint is whatever makes the issue unresolvable. Ask: what would have to change structurally for this conversation to stop recurring?

**Workarounds.** Every manual process that exists because something upstream failed is a constraint. The workaround tells you the symptom is visible enough that someone built a patch for it. The patch points directly at the structural failure underneath.

**Sausage-making.** Every organization has processes nobody would want a customer, a board member, or a new hire to watch. The discomfort you feel imagining that observation is pointing at the constraint. Name it.

**Turnover.** When the same role keeps bouncing people out, the role is the symptom. The constraint is the structural failure the role was built on top of. Nobody can succeed in a role where the work was never designed to succeed.

### Meridian Manufacturing.

Consider Meridian Manufacturing, the fictional company we introduced earlier. Their team's symptom was "our quoting takes too long." The constraint underneath it was Elena Ruiz, the VP of Operations. Every quote passed through her because she was the only person who held the customer-specific pricing, material lead-time knowledge, and historical job context simultaneously. That constraint cost $558K per year in lost revenue, misallocated time, and floor underutilization.

Signal makes you stop at the symptom long enough to find the constraint underneath it, then put a number on what that constraint is costing. Until both moves are complete, you are not at Signal yet.

### Trace each symptom to its root.

Most of what you surface is symptoms. The way down to the constraint underneath is a conversation, not a worksheet. Take one candidate and keep asking why until the answer stops moving.

1. Why is this happening? The first answer is almost always another symptom.
2. Why is that the case? Closer.
3. Why does that happen? Now you're near the structure.
4. What's underneath that? The structural cause.
5. What's the root? The constraint itself.

Run it as a back-and-forth with the room, not a form one person fills out alone. Two people rarely trace the same symptom to the same place. The CEO names one cause, the manager closest to the work names another, and the gap between their answers is usually where the constraint is hiding. Keep going until the room lands in the same spot.

**The stop rule.** You've reached the constraint when the answer points to a workflow, a handoff, a missing system, or a structural gap. You have not reached it when the answer is a person's name or a market condition. If the honest answer to your last "why" is a name, "because Sarah is the only one who knows," go one layer down. The constraint isn't Sarah. It's that critical knowledge lives in one head with no system to distribute it. The structure put Sarah in that position, and the structure is what a Sprint can fix.

{{< excalidraw ch04-five-whys-chain "The Five Whys traced on the PT clinic: from the symptom (efficiency 58–63%) down to the structural constraint, with the stop rule that keeps you off the people layer." >}}

:::{.callout-tip}
## Pro Tip
Push past the person to the structure. The most common way this conversation stalls is stopping at "the wrong person is in the seat." The seat is rarely the root; the structure that built it is. EOS calls this root-cause work Identify, the first move of its IDS track, and Mark O'Donnell's *Issues!* is the best field guide to running it — read it for the craft, then take the layer past the seat that it tends to skip.
:::

:::{.callout-note}
## Action Step
Take your top three candidates. Trace each one to root with the Five Whys, out loud, with the people closest to the work in the room. Cross off anything that bottoms out at a market condition, a personality, or a problem you can't put a number on.
:::

## The PT clinic that almost opened a sixth location.

Julie sat in on a meeting with a PT clinic operator that was forty-five minutes into a conversation about opening their sixth location. Site selection, lease terms, staffing — everyone around the table owned a piece of the vision.

Julie asked what their clinical efficiency rating was across the five clinics they already had. The room went quiet. Nobody knew. Julie walked to the whiteboard, drew the formula, and they worked the numbers together. The number came out between 58 and 63 percent depending on the location. Industry standard for expansion is 83.

{{< excalidraw ch04-efficiency-gap "Clinical efficiency gap: actual 58–63% vs. expansion threshold of 83%." >}}

Julie put the marker down and said: we've spent four hours today discussing a sixth facility, and the five you already own are running at 60 percent efficiency. You're not ready to expand. Stop that conversation.

The room agreed. What was the constraint underneath the efficiency gap? Scheduling. When patients canceled, nobody filled those slots fast enough. The front desk was running the replacement loop manually — checking the waitlist in the EHR, calling patients one by one, hoping someone could come in on short notice. A backlog of people who wanted appointments existed in the system. The process connecting them to the open slots was broken. Thirty-seven to forty-two percent of cancellation slots went unfilled, despite a waitlist of patients who wanted those appointments.

The expansion plan was a symptom. The scheduling loop was the constraint. The gap between 60 and 83 tells you which one to work on.

Here is the blank Constraint Statement template. Fill it in for your own validated constraint as you work through this chapter. The PT clinic populated version follows directly below it as a worked reference.

| Field | Your constraint |
|---|---|
| **Constraint** _(the one anchoring sentence)_ |  |
| **Where it lives** _(function, workflow, locations)_ |  |
| **Duration** _(how long has it been this way)_ |  |
| **Quantified cost** _(dollars, hours, throughput per period)_ |  |
| **Validating evidence** _(who confirmed it, with what data)_ |  |

The anchoring sentence at the top follows the Function / Outcome / Root cause / Cost structure from earlier in the chapter: "[Function] cannot [desired outcome] because [root cause], which costs us approximately [X] per [time period]."

Here is what that template looked like populated for the PT clinic:

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Constraint** | Patient cancellation slots are filled manually by front desk staff, leaving 37-42% of slots unfilled despite a backlog of patients waiting for appointments. |
| **Where it lives** | Front desk → scheduling workflow → manual process of matching cancellations to the waitlist. All 5 locations. |
| **Duration** | ~2 years (since third location opened). Workaround normalized — staff treats manual slot-filling as their job, not as a broken process. |
| **Quantified cost** | Efficiency at 58-63% vs. 83% expansion threshold. ~$420K/year in unrealized revenue (22 unfilled slots/week x $75 avg visit x 5 locations x 50 weeks). Blocking planned 6th location — est. $200K+ in delayed expansion revenue. |
| **Validating evidence** | Efficiency calculated live in leadership meeting. Front desk confirmed manual process. Waitlist exists in EHR but not connected to cancellation notifications. No staff member disputed the gap. |

That's the artifact. Anybody in that company could read it and understand what the Sprint was solving without asking a follow-up question.

## How to run Signal yourself.

Signal is a facilitated conversation with your leadership team.

{{< excalidraw ch04-constraint-path "The path Signal walks: surface the candidates, trace each to root, confirm the load-bearing one, quantify the cost, and lock a single constraint on paper." >}}

### Step 1: Surface the candidates.

Before you can pick one constraint, you need an honest inventory of what's broken or slow. This is the Issue Surfacer conversation. Ask the room questions like these (use them as a starting set, not a script):

1. What are we working around? What manual process exists because something upstream failed?
2. What does a new person always find confusing in their first ninety days?
3. What process would we never let a customer watch?
4. Where do we keep losing the same person or role? Turnover clusters around constraints.
5. What conversation keeps coming up in meetings but never gets resolved?

Write everything down without filtering. Aim for five to ten candidates. If you have fewer than three, you haven't been honest enough. If you have more than fifteen, you're listing symptoms — group them.

:::{.callout-note}
## Action Step
Open a whiteboard or shared doc. List candidates using the five questions above. No filtering, no debate about whether something belongs. Write everything down.
:::

### Step 2: Trace symptoms to constraints.

Most of your candidates are symptoms. Trace your top three to root with the Five Whys (described above). Run each as a conversation with the people closest to the work, not a form filled out alone. Cross off anything that bottoms out at a market condition, a personality conflict, or a problem you can't quantify.

### Picking among candidates.

When the Five Whys leaves you with more than one surviving candidate, the pain level alone won't tell you which to attack first. You need a tiebreaker. Here's the rubric we use with every team that finds itself in that spot.

1. **Foundation first.** Some candidates unblock the others. Constraint Clarity is almost always the foundation: until the leadership team agrees on the one bottleneck, every other candidate is being evaluated against a moving target. If a candidate is a precondition for the others, it goes first.
2. **Highest pain inside reach.** Of the remaining candidates, pick the one closest to the operational pain that brought you to the conversation. Not the most interesting candidate, not the easiest one, the one that sits on the workflow that's actually hurting.
3. **Smallest gap to resolution.** When two candidates are roughly tied on pain, pick the one with the smallest distance to a locked constraint. You've got partial answers, partial documentation, or a person who already knows the workflow. Less distance means a faster lock, and a fast lock builds credibility for the harder work behind it.
4. **Owner in the room.** Don't pick a candidate that nobody on the leadership team owns. If you can't name the person who'll move it, you've picked a wish, not a constraint.
5. **Two-quarter horizon.** Pick the candidate you can plausibly lock and Sprint inside two quarters with the team you've got. If it's longer than that, the work is too big to be a single Sprint and needs to be broken down into a tighter constraint first.

Apply the rubric in order. The first candidate that passes all five is where you start.

### Meridian applied.

Meridian's Issue Surfacer conversation surfaced several candidates. Their Five Whys work left three: the quoting bottleneck, the workflow visibility gap, and incomplete cost tracking. Which one first wasn't obvious from the symptoms alone.

Foundation first: the quoting bottleneck had already surfaced in every L10, but the leadership team hadn't formally committed to it as the single constraint. Locking that agreement was the precondition for everything else. Workflow Visibility and cost tracking both depended on the team agreeing on what constraint they were mapping and measuring. Quoting passed all five criteria: clear pain, clear owner in Elena, two-quarter horizon, and unlocked both remaining candidates once the bottleneck was named.

Meridian's starting point: lock the quoting bottleneck as the constraint, then map the workflow around it. Those two moves created the foundation for everything that followed in Source and Design.

:::{.callout-tip}
## Pro Tip
When the tiebreaker doesn't produce a clear winner (two candidates pass all five criteria), go with the one whose cost estimate is harder to dispute. The number that survives scrutiny is the one the room will hold each other to.
:::

### Step 3: Run the five constraint questions.

Walk each surviving candidate through these five questions, in order. Do not skip ahead.

**Question 1: What is the problem in one sentence?** Force precision. A usable statement reads: "The VP of Operations is the sole bottleneck for quoting — every quote requires her direct involvement, resulting in 3-5 day turnaround versus the 24-48 hour industry standard, costing $558K per year."

**Question 2: Where does it live in the organization?** Name the team, the workflow, and the handoff. If it crosses departments, name the boundary where the breakdown occurs. Test: could you walk to the place in your building where this problem lives?

**Question 3: How long has it existed?** Months? Years? Since a system change? Since a departure? Duration tells you two things: how deeply embedded the workarounds are, and whether the team has normalized the problem. Anything over twelve months has almost certainly been normalized.

**Question 4: What does it cost?** In hours per week, dollars per quarter, margin lost, or deals not closed. This must be a number. This is the gate. Without a quantified cost, you can't act on it.

If the data isn't clean, estimate:

- **Hours:** "How many hours per week does this person or team spend on this?" multiplied by hourly loaded cost, multiplied by 52 weeks.
- **Deals:** "How many quotes or opportunities did we lose or not pursue because of this?" multiplied by average deal value.
- **Margin:** "What would our margin be on this line if this constraint didn't exist?" minus current margin.
- **Speed:** "How many days does this add to our cycle?" multiplied by cost of delay per day.

**Question 5: If this constraint were removed, what would actually change?** Be specific. What would be different in the next ninety days? Which number would move, and by how much?

{{< excalidraw ch04-five-signal-questions "The five constraint questions in order, with Question 4 — cost — as the gate you can't pass without a number." >}}

:::{.callout-tip}
## Pro Tip
Question 4 is where Signal lives or dies. "$558K per year in lost revenue, misallocated time, and floor underutilization — concentrated in the quoting workflow" is a constraint you can act on. "It's expensive" is not. The number tells you whether the constraint is worth a Sprint, and gives the Deliver phase a target to measure against.
:::

### Step 4: Pick one. Lock it.

When you've walked the candidates through all five questions, one will have the strongest answers — the clearest location, the longest history, the largest cost. That is the constraint you bring to Source. Write it in a single sentence, surrounded by the evidence that validates it, using the one-page template from earlier in this chapter.

Two tests confirm you're at root constraint and not still looking at a symptom:

**The lever test.** Look at your candidate list and ask: "If we solved this one, how many of the others get easier or go away on their own?" A root constraint is load-bearing. Solving it moves multiple problems. If the answer is "none of them," you're likely holding a symptom. If the answer is "several," you've found the right one.

**The restate test.** Say out loud: "All of these problems stem from [your candidate]. This is actually the problem we need to solve." If the room resists and people reach for other causes, you don't have the root yet. Keep asking why. If the room agrees, you're there.

Read the completed statement back to the room. Ask: "Is this the thing?" If anyone hesitates, you're not locked. Keep refining until the room actually agrees.

:::{.callout-note}
## Action Step
Fill in the one-page Constraint Statement template for your chosen constraint. Read it aloud to the team. If the room can't agree that this is the one constraint worth a Sprint, you're not done. Keep working until you have real agreement — the kind where people nod because the math convinced them, not because the meeting has gone long.
:::

### Step 5: Run the failure mode checklist.

Before you call Signal complete, check for these common failure modes:

- **Too abstract.** "We need better processes" is not a constraint. Can you point to a specific workflow?
- **Too many.** You wrote down three constraints. Pick one. A Sprint that solves three problems solves none.
- **No number.** The cost field is empty or says "significant." Go back to question four.
- **Dominant personality resolved the ambiguity.** The most senior person in the room named the symptom first. Everyone nodded. The meeting moved on. The structural cause never surfaced. This is the most common Signal failure in well-run leadership teams. Ask: "Did we pick this because the data points here, or because the first person to speak named it?"
- **Named the person instead of the structure.** "The constraint is Susie" is never the answer. Susie operates inside a structure. If Susie is failing, the structure failed first. The constraint is whatever the structure does that makes it impossible for anyone in Susie's position to succeed. This isn't a defense of poor performance. It's a discipline that keeps Signal from becoming a performance review.
- **Solved the symptom.** Your constraint sentence describes what you feel, not what causes it. Run Five Whys one more time.
- **Can't be solved by a Sprint.** The constraint is "our market is shrinking" or "our founder won't delegate." These are real, but they're upstream of this book. Signal is for operational constraints a Sprint can address.

If any of these are true, go back. The gate is real. Passing through it with a bad Constraint Statement costs more than the time it takes to fix it.

## Where the constraint comes from inside an *EOS or Scaling Up shop*.

If your company runs on EOS, Scaling Up, or a similar cadence-based management system, you already have most of Signal's inputs sitting on a whiteboard or in a shared doc. You just have to know where to look — and then run the constraint questions against what you find. If your team hasn't built the muscle of surfacing and articulating issues yet, that's the skill to develop first, and the trace method earlier in this chapter is where to start.

**The Issues list** (an EOS term) is the most obvious input. Every L10, every weekly tactical, every quarterly review produces a list of issues the team has been carrying. Most of them are symptoms. A few of them, traced honestly, are constraints. Walk that list and ask, for each one: is this a root cause or a symptom? When you find one that survives that question, one you can locate in a specific workflow with a duration and a cost, run the five constraint questions against it. That becomes your constraint candidate.

**Stalled rocks** are the second input. A rock that has been carried for three quarters without progress is almost always sitting on top of a constraint that nobody named. The rock is the symptom. The constraint is whatever is preventing the rock from moving. Ask: what would have to be true for this rock to move on its own? The answer to that question is usually the constraint.

**The headcount conversation** is the third. Every time the org reaches for a hire, a constraint is hiding underneath. The work is real. The team is stretched. The default move is to add a person. But under that conversation is a workflow that was never designed for the volume it's now carrying. Before you post the role, run the constraint questions: what is the constraint generating the demand for a new hire? Where does it live? What has it cost this quarter? Half the time, naming it changes what you do next. The other half, you still hire — but against a redesigned workflow rather than the one that's already failing.

:::{.callout-note}
## Action Step
Pull your current issues list, your stalled rocks, and any open headcount requests. Pick the one that feels most expensive and run it through the five constraint questions. If you can put a real number on it, you have a constraint worth a Sprint. If you can't, keep walking the list.
:::

## The failure mode that looks like work.

Skipping Signal doesn't look like failure. It looks like activity: tools being evaluated, demos on Fridays, somebody prompting in Slack. None of it is Signal. The org hasn't named a single constraint it's committed to solving.

This shows up in well-run EOS shops. The leadership team sits down to work through the issues list. Someone with authority names the problem. The room nods. They move to solutions. Nobody asks whether the named problem is actually the problem. This isn't Signal. The dominant personality resolved the discomfort of ambiguity, and the underlying constraint is still there, unnamed, costing the same amount it was costing before the meeting started.

## With the constraint locked, you can map *what surrounds it*.

The one-page Constraint Statement is the handoff to Source. With the constraint named, quantified, and validated, the next move is to map the knowledge and data that surround it — what the organization actually knows about the problem, where that knowledge lives, who holds it, and what is missing.

If you can't hand someone that one page and have them understand what the Sprint is solving without asking a follow-up question, you're not done with Signal. Go back. The gate is real.

That is Source.

## Reflection Questions

1. Run the Issue Surfacer questions on your company right now: what process would you never let a customer watch? Where does your team keep losing the same person or role? What conversation keeps coming up in L10s but never gets resolved? Which answer feels most expensive?
2. The PT clinic was forty-five minutes into planning a sixth location before someone asked what clinical efficiency rating was. Where in your company is your team solving a symptom while the actual constraint runs untouched underneath it?
3. Apply the Five Whys to your top constraint candidate. Does the fifth "why" point to a workflow, a handoff, or a structural gap — or does it point to a person? If it points to a person, reframe: what system failure put that person in the position of being the only one who knows?
4. Can you fill in all five fields of the one-page Constraint Statement template today — constraint sentence, location, duration, quantified cost with math, and validating evidence? If the cost field is empty, what data would you need to fill it in, and who owns that data?
5. If you polled your leadership team individually and asked "what is the ONE operational problem AI should solve for us?" — how many different answers would you get? Run the poll before your next L10 and compare results.
